blocks.text: Imagine a city map with intersections as points and roads as lines connecting them. This is a graph, a fundamental structure in discrete mathematics, modeling relationships and connections.

blocks.markdown: Graphs are mathematical structures used to model pairwise relations between objects. A graph consists of vertices (or nodes) and edges (or arcs) connecting these vertices. In this lesson, we will explore how to represent graphs using adjacency matrices and adjacency lists, and how to apply the handshake lemma.

blocks.title: Graph
blocks.text: A graph $G$ is an ordered pair $G = (V, E)$, where $V$ is a set of vertices and $E$ is a set of edges, which are 2-element subsets of $V$ for undirected graphs, or ordered pairs of $V$ for directed graphs.

blocks.markdown: Graphs can be **directed** or **undirected**. In a directed graph, edges have a direction, from one vertex to another. In an undirected graph, edges do not have a direction.

blocks.title: Degree
blocks.text: The degree of a vertex in an undirected graph is the number of edges incident to it. In a directed graph, the in-degree is the number of incoming edges, and the out-degree is the number of outgoing edges.

blocks.markdown: To represent graphs, we often use **adjacency matrices** or **adjacency lists**. Each has its own advantages depending on the graph's density.

blocks.title: Adjacency Matrix
blocks.text: An adjacency matrix is a square matrix used to represent a finite graph. The elements of the matrix indicate whether pairs of vertices are adjacent or not in the graph.

blocks.title: Adjacency Matrix
blocks.prompt: Consider a graph with vertices $V = \{A, B, C\}$ and edges $E = \{(A, B), (B, C)\}$. Construct the adjacency matrix.

steps.text: List the vertices in a fixed order: $A, B, C$.
Create a 3x3 matrix since there are 3 vertices.
For each pair of vertices $(i, j)$, set the matrix entry $M[i][j] = 1$ if there is an edge from $i$ to $j$, otherwise set it to 0.

blocks.title: Adjacency List
blocks.text: An adjacency list represents a graph as an array of lists. The array index represents the vertex, and each element in its list represents the vertices adjacent to it.

blocks.title: Adjacency List
blocks.prompt: Construct the adjacency list for the same graph with vertices $V = \{A, B, C\}$ and edges $E = \{(A, B), (B, C)\}$.

steps.text: Create a list for each vertex.
For each edge $(i, j)$, add vertex $j$ to the list of vertex $i$.

blocks.answer: The adjacency list is $A: [B], B: [C], C: []$.

blocks.markdown: The **handshake lemma** is a fundamental result in graph theory, stating that the sum of the degrees of all vertices in an undirected graph is twice the number of edges.

blocks.title: Handshake Lemma
blocks.text: In any undirected graph, the sum of the degrees of all vertices is equal to twice the number of edges: $\sum_{v \in V} \deg(v) = 2|E|$.

points: Graphs can be represented as adjacency matrices or adjacency lists.
The handshake lemma relates the sum of vertex degrees to twice the number of edges.
